brief.head: The university waqf
brief.text: A waqf set up to build water foun­tains keeps its cap­i­tal after piped water ar­rives. Universities’ vast en­dow­ments, Amit Varma said, are much the same: dead cap­i­tal. {024-C13}

brief.head: Write it, think it
brief.text: Writing clearly is not just a sign of clear think­ing, Amit Varma said after George Orwell. Forcing your­self to write clearly forces you to think clearly. {024-C11}

brief.head: Let firms fund it
brief.text: Corporations make mer­i­to­cratic fun­ders of re­search, Ajay Shah said, be­cause they pose con­crete prob­lems. Government fund­ing is a state-capacity prob­lem; phi­lan­thropy plays too safe. {024-C03}

brief.head: Who are we, anyway?
brief.text: Firms and gov­ern­ments must keep ask­ing who they are and what they are doing wrong, Ajay Shah said. Too often they be­come con­tests for power. {024-C06}

brief.head: Communities of choice
brief.text: Toxic as Twitter is, Amit Varma said, it lets him watch the best minds think aloud every morn­ing. Most of his friends he met be­cause of the in­ter­net. {024-C14}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on knowledge and its keepers
lead.head: The academy fails its own exam

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 24

body: Ajay Shah, Amit Varma said, likes to tease him for hav­ing stud­ied noth­ing while Shah is a card-carrying econ­o­mist with a PhD. Yet here Shah was, agree­ing that aca­demics is bro­ken and de­grees mean noth­ing. “Across twenty short episodes,” Shah said, “Amit has changed my views.” {024-J01}
The sub­ject was the knowl­edge so­ci­ety, and why its in­sti­tu­tions are fail­ing.

Knowledge, Shah said, is “the great nu­clear re­ac­tor run­ning in­side the en­tire mod­ern world”. Every knowl­edge or­gan­i­sa­tion, he ar­gued, has a three-part mis­sion. “So we are here to make knowl­edge, to dif­fuse knowl­edge, and to link up knowl­edge to ac­tion to trans­late knowl­edge into a bet­ter world.” {024-C01}
All three pil­lars, he said, are a lit­tle bro­ken.
## Three cracks

On the mak­ing of knowl­edge, Shah de­scribed a pro­fes­sion that has traded cu­rios­ity for ca­reer lad­ders. The ques­tion is no longer what im­por­tant prob­lem one can solve, but how to get into a par­tic­u­lar jour­nal.

In eco­nom­ics, which he called the most bro­ken jour­nal process of all, an idea that took a week can take five to eight years to pub­lish. “People prob­a­bly get three good days a year of imag­in­ing,” he said, “and three hun­dred and sixty-two days a year are just spent on mun­dane shit of schmooz­ing, of net­work­ing, of fig­ur­ing out what ed­i­tors like, what ref­er­ees like.” {024-C02}
Most pub­lished pa­pers, he added, are never cited.

On the spread­ing of knowl­edge, the uni­ver­sity has be­come a brand-name fac­tory. Students want the de­gree that gets them a job at Google. Parents get four years of day­care; em­ploy­ers get a sig­nal.
The brand it­self adds lit­tle, Shah said. “If you take any IIT grad­u­ate, and if they did not at­tend IIT, you know what, their life would more or less be the same.”
Nor can learn­ing be crammed into four years, he said, when peo­ple live longer and the world keeps chang­ing.
## The view from out­side

Varma, who said he was not a crea­ture of that world, put it more bluntly. “I think aca­demics is ut­terly ir­rel­e­vant. It’s a cir­cle jerk. It’s pompous old farts talk­ing to other pompous old farts.”
He took aim at turgid prose, at silos and at con­form­ity.
But he was not in de­spair. Anyone with hunger can now learn from YouTube, pod­casts and books, and cre­ators own the means of pro­duc­tion.
“We are play­ing the long game, we are build­ing a repos­i­tory of con­tent, and we are try­ing to cre­ate in dif­fer­ent ways a com­mu­nity of thinkers,” he said. {024-C16}
His imag­ined viewer is a fif­teen-year-old girl in a re­mote Indian town who will be prime min­is­ter in thirty years.
## Mind the se­lec­tors

Shah’s part­ing thought came from cricket. A player’s worth mat­ters only once it reaches the se­lec­tors, and in academia, he said, the deep­est fail­ures lie in who gets se­lected, pro­moted and funded. {024-C07}
Admissions re­ward reg­i­men­ta­tion and good grades rather than cu­rios­ity, and the re­sult is safe, bu­reau­cratic peo­ple in­stead of an Einstein or a Ramanujan.

He also ar­gued that credit is widely shared, and that win­ner-takes-all prizes make peo­ple hoard ideas. Varma, twice a win­ner of the Bastiat Prize, wanted a free mar­ket in prizes rather than none. “But do not take my two can­dle­sticks away from me,” he said.

second.label: Einstein’s day job
second.head: A clerk with no budget
second.deck: Ajay Shah’s model researcher was a patent clerk with zero funding

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Einstein the patent clerk

body: Ajay Shah’s ideal of how knowl­edge should be made is Albert Einstein, a full-time clerk in a patent of­fice. “Just imag­ine he’s doing a day job in a patent of­fice, he can’t be very well paid and he has zero bud­gets, he has no fund­ing,” Shah said. Einstein be­came one of the most in­flu­en­tial sci­en­tists ever. {024-S02}
Shah apol­o­gised to view­ers who work in patent of­fices. His point was that Einstein, like Ramanujan, was driven by an inner hunger: cu­rios­ity and pas­sion, pur­sued for their own sake.

Modern aca­demics is in­stead a game of climb­ing ca­reer lad­ders, chas­ing jour­nal pub­li­ca­tions and fund­ing. So, Shah said, “we get dull peo­ple join­ing, or bright peo­ple have the spark smashed out of them”. {#spark}

quote.text: We want thinkers and in­tel­lec­tu­als who have their inner fire of cu­rios­ity and of pas­sion

third.head: Knowledge in every pore

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Vajpayee’s knowledge speech

body: Ajay Shah re­mem­bers a speech by Vajpayee, from around 2002 or 2003, with some beau­ti­ful para­graphs on the knowl­edge econ­omy. Its mes­sage was that knowl­edge is not some­thing to hide in a uni­ver­sity. {024-S01}

“The knowl­edge econ­omy should fill every pore of our bod­ies,” Shah re­called. Knowledge should cast aside su­per­sti­tion in in­di­vid­ual lives. It should feed into firms, mak­ing them high-productivity firms, and into the state, so that it prac­tises ev­i­dence-based pol­icy.
Shah set this against a crude view of pol­i­tics found in India: you win elec­tions, and then you send agen­cies after your ri­vals. That view, he con­ceded, has a germ of truth in it.
The power-and-coercion view of the state, he said, “is a royal road to ruin. And that is what un­der­de­vel­op­ment and the third world is all about.” {#ruin}

p2.deck: How knowledge is made, spread and put to use, and why the hosts think creators are taking over {024-C01}

from1.head: The academy fails its own exam

quote.text: It stopped be­com­ing what’s an im­por­tant prob­lem that I can solve. It’s be­come how do I hack into X jour­nal and get that paper.

box.title: The three pillars
box.text: Ajay Shah thinks all three pil­lars of a knowl­edge so­ci­ety are a lit­tle bro­ken. They are to make knowl­edge, to dif­fuse it, and to turn it into a bet­ter world through firms and the state. That, he said, should be every uni­ver­sity trustee’s mis­sion state­ment. {024-C01}

sections.label: Pillar One
sections.head: Shut up and get the pub
sections.caption: the journal game
body: Ajay Shah has spent more years in uni­ver­si­ties than he cares to admit, and he wanted the hosts to turn the an­a­lyt­i­cal lens on them­selves. If they can make fun of home­opa­thy and hy­dro­pon­ics, he said, they should make fun of academia too.

Much of the world’s knowl­edge, he said, is shaped by jour­nals and fund­ing. Researchers no longer ask what im­por­tant prob­lem they can solve; they study what ed­i­tors and ref­er­ees like, “a bit like lem­mings”.

The irony, Shah said, is that pa­pers in the top-ranked jour­nals are in many ways the less good ones, be­cause more en­ergy went into hack­ing the sys­tem. Of all fields, he thinks eco­nom­ics has the most bro­ken jour­nal process. {024-C02}
## Publication ori­en­ta­tion

Young re­searchers meet a dreaded phrase, “pub­li­ca­tion ori­en­ta­tion”, which older aca­demics use to beat the ide­al­ism out of them. “You’re sup­posed to or­ga­nize your life around shut up and get the pub,” Shah said. {024-J14}
Funding works best, he ar­gued, when it comes from cor­po­ra­tions, which are mer­i­to­cratic and pose con­crete prob­lems, such as mak­ing a wid­get work at 256 de­grees. {#widget}

~ Philanthropy, by con­trast, chases feel-good goals and plays safe. “James Watt ar­guably did more for poor peo­ple in India than Mother Teresa,” Shah said. “But most phi­lan­thropists are not suf­fi­ciently in­tel­lec­tual to see these links.” {024-C03}

quote.text: It stopped be­com­ing what’s an im­por­tant prob­lem that I can solve. It’s be­come how do I hack into X jour­nal and get that paper.

sections.label: Pillar Two
sections.head: Four years of daycare
sections.caption: credentialism and lifelong learning
body: The dif­fu­sion of knowl­edge, Ajay Shah said, has de­gen­er­ated into cre­den­tial­ism. Students have no in­ter­est in the knowl­edge; they want the de­gree that gets them a job with Google.

Universities have no­ticed what their brand names are worth, and their prices have crept up. The hosts’ friend Josh Felman told Shah that putting one child through col­lege in America “in­volves buy­ing one brand new BMW car every year and rolling it off the edge of a cliff”. {024-J04}
The money buys gyms, lux­u­ri­ous hous­ing and five-star fa­cil­i­ties. Students are made to work 12 hours a day in reg­i­mented ways, which, Shah said, breeds medi­ocrity. {#twelve}
The real bar­gain: par­ents get day­care for four years, the chil­dren get a *chapa*, a stamp, and a job fol­lows.
## Kindling, not fill­ing
Learning, for Shah, never fin­ishes. He of­fered “a beau­ti­ful quo­ta­tion”: “the process of ed­u­ca­tion is not fill­ing a pail, the process of ed­u­ca­tion is kin­dling a fire.” {024-J15}

The uni­ver­sity is an in­dus­trial-era con­struct, he said, from when peo­ple stopped work at 55 or 60. The hosts had told their cam­era­man Vaishnav that he would live to 120, and over a hun­dred years, ev­ery­thing about him will change. {#vaishnav}
~ Even the hosts, Shah noted, had to learn at a ripe age what it means to make a YouTube show.

quote.text: I can dis­play for­mal com­pe­tence. I can pass any exam, but I’ve not ac­tu­ally un­der­stood things.

sections.label: The outsider’s view
sections.head: Turgid by design
sections.caption: turgid prose and conformity
body: Amit Varma’s writ­ing stu­dents often ask what to do about the turgid prose academia ex­pects of them. He points them to an essay by the philoso­pher Agnes Callard, *Publish and Perish*, which ex­plains it with an economist’s tool: in­cen­tives. {024-R05}
Tenure re­quires pub­li­ca­tions in cer­tain jour­nals, and those jour­nals re­ward their own con­ven­tions, turgid writ­ing among them, along with the in­tel­lec­tual fash­ions of the day.

Varma’s ad­vice has two parts. Clear aca­demic writ­ing is pos­si­ble, so find mod­els such as the econ­o­mists Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok. And if a ca­reer de­mands the style, use it know­ingly and keep it out of ev­ery­thing else. {024-C10}
## Wheat in Arizona
His other com­plaints are silos and con­form­ity. Dig deep enough, he said, and “you’ll be writ­ing about wheat pro­duc­tion in Arizona be­tween the years 1863 to 1865”. {024-J07}

Young peo­ple ar­rive as self-declared rebels and con­form any­way. A paper by Paul Smaldino and Joshua Epstein puts it in its title: *Social Conformity Despite Individual Preferences for Distinctiveness*. {024-R07}

~ The cure, for Varma, is many frames and a mul­ti­dis­ci­plinary out­look, the motto be­hind the show’s name. “If you are in the busi­ness of knowl­edge, then you can­not have one frame, one ham­mer for every nail.” {024-C12}

quote.text: But know why you’re doing it and don’t let those habits seep into the other writ­ing that you do.

sections.label: The golden age
sections.head: No gatekeeper required
sections.caption: the creator’s golden age
body: For most of his­tory, Amit Varma said, your knowl­edge was lim­ited to what the peo­ple around you told you. Even after Gutenberg, only a small elite read, and uni­ver­si­ties made sense as places where knowl­edge and bright minds gath­ered.
Not any more. Anyone with the hunger and the spark can learn from YouTube, pod­casts and books. Varma said he had told Vaishnav that he wished he were fif­teen today. {#fifteen}

Spreading what you knew used to mean pass­ing gate­keep­ers, with their bi­ases, their scarce space and their bud­gets. Now cre­ators own the means of pro­duc­tion, and niches no one knew ex­isted can sud­denly ap­pear.
## Ninety-five per cent
Sniffiness about pop­u­lar YouTubers misses Sturgeon’s Law, Varma said: “Ninety five per­cent of ev­ery­thing is crap,” and it has al­ways been so. {024-J19}
Ajay Shah added a thought on the self-taught ge­nius: “Today, Ramanujan would have been dol­ing out his gems, one blog ar­ti­cle at a time.” {024-J10}
~ Varma agreed. Ramanujan, he said, had to re­dis­cover things that were al­ready known, and with ac­cess to knowl­edge he might have learned faster.

quote.text: You no longer need to say XYZ is bad. That sucks. You can now say sure XYZ is bad, so what? I’ll do bet­ter.

sections.label: The long game
sections.head: Picasso had help
sections.caption: credit, prizes and selectors
body: Ajay Shah bor­rowed a les­son from cricket. A player’s value be­comes a pro­gramme for ac­tion only when it reaches the se­lec­tors, and in academia, too, the root cause lies with those who se­lect, pro­mote and fund. {024-C07}

Admissions de­mand reg­i­men­ta­tion and good grades, and India’s pop­ulist in­sis­tence on ob­jec­tive exams makes things worse. The best peo­ple, he said, are not com­ing into the knowl­edge busi­ness.
## The last run­ner
Credit, Shah ar­gued, is dis­persed. Picasso did not step out of thin air and in­vent cu­bism; he picked up pieces from the many peo­ple around him. {#picasso}

Prizes re­ward only the run­ner who takes the baton across the fin­ish line. “If you and I are in a race for a Nobel Prize, then I’ll be hoard­ing my ideas and you’ll be hoard­ing your ideas.” {024-C08}
He would ex­tend au­thor­ship even to some­one met once at a bi­cy­cle re­pair shop, if the con­ver­sa­tion shaped the paper.
Amit Varma, who has won the Bastiat Prize twice, an­swered with com­pe­ti­tion rather than abo­li­tion: let any­one fund a prize for what­ever they value. {024-C09}
~ Shah quoted a song­writer both hosts think a lot about: “and I won and I won big once. And I paid the cost.” {024-J17}

quote.text: So that one who wins big should be seen in the con­text of all the other strivers.
It takes years of ded­i­ca­tion and at­ten­tion and focus and a pas­sion for know­ing, through which, bit by bit the veils part and the uni­verse re­veals its knowl­edge to you.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A mathematician, a podcaster, a prize-winner and Adam Smith’s bookshelf

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a mathematician who said no to everything
stories.head: A proof needs no prize
body: Grigori Perelman, as Ajay Shah tells it, is a great math­e­ma­ti­cian and a charm­ing guy. He lives in Moscow with his mother, and walks in the for­est gath­er­ing mush­rooms.
He also did some great work, which, Shah said, would take many min­utes to ex­plain. Perelman wrote a paper and put it up on a web­site, arXiv, and was done.

Why not pub­lish it in a jour­nal, peo­ple asked. Perelman’s reply, in Shah’s telling: “Either the proof is right or the proof is wrong. If the proof is right, I am a good math­e­ma­ti­cian and for hun­dreds of years this will be re­mem­bered. If the proof is wrong, this stuff should just be thrown away.” {024-S05}
A journal’s brand name, he rea­soned, could make no dif­fer­ence to the qual­ity of the work. If peo­ple liked the paper, they would read it.
Then came fame, and prizes. The or­gan­is­ers of a Clay award of a mil­lion dol­lars qui­etly asked whether he would come and col­lect it. He said no. They asked again. He said no again.

Prizes, he ex­plained, give ex­ces­sively dis­pro­por­tion­ate re­wards to some peo­ple and dam­age the col­lab­o­ra­tion DNA of the whole com­mu­nity. He had stood on the shoul­ders of many oth­ers who got no prize. And he lived with his mother, walked in the for­est and col­lected mush­rooms. What would he do with a mil­lion dol­lars?

~ He never ap­peared for the prize. Shah’s own worry about prizes, he said, was an idea he stole from Perelman, who opened his eyes to how one person’s award leaves ev­ery­one else a lit­tle in the shadow. {#stole}
stories.why: Perelman cut out both mid­dle­men of aca­demic credit, the jour­nal and the prize. For Shah, his re­fusal shows how win­ner-takes-all re­wards re­shape ev­ery­one else’s in­cen­tives and dam­age the col­lab­o­ra­tion on which knowl­edge de­pends. {024-C08}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma called it a “mag­nif­i­cent in­spir­ing story”, and then, as a two-time prize win­ner, begged to dif­fer.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Grigori Perelman’s refusal

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on writing before and after the gatekeepers
stories.head: No editor, no word limit
body: In the 1990s, Amit Varma said, a writer with some­thing to say sent an ar­ti­cle to a news­pa­per like the *Times of India* or the *Hindustan Times*. The paper sold readers’ eye­balls to ad­ver­tis­ers, and the writer got a tiny chunk of the money.
Then Varma be­came one of the early blog­gers. He no longer needed a gate­keeper, a news cycle or a limit of 800 or 900 words, and he could talk di­rectly with read­ers. {#words}

Thirty years ago, he said, he would have gone to a radio com­pany, the only audio there was, and pro­posed an eight-hour pod­cast of long con­ver­sa­tions with bor­ing aca­demics. “I would have been laughed out of the room.” {024-S04}
~ Today he is a pro­fes­sional pod­caster, and all the money he makes comes di­rectly from lis­ten­ers and view­ers.
stories.why: Creators now own the means of pro­duc­tion for ideas. Formats no­body imag­ined can find an au­di­ence with­out ask­ing a gatekeeper’s per­mis­sion, and the money can come straight from the peo­ple who lis­ten. {024-C15}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the eight-hour podcast

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the award that kept him going
stories.head: Lonely road, two prizes
body: The Bastiat Prize, named after Amit Varma’s hero Frédéric Bastiat, goes to a jour­nal­ist who up­holds the ideals of a free so­ci­ety. Varma first won it in 2007, when, he said, he was lit­er­ally the only per­son in India writ­ing about free­dom.
“It was a lonely jour­ney,” he said. “Everybody abused me in those days.” The $10,000 that came with the prize meant a lot to him too. {#tenk}

Then he re­nounced the world for five years to play poker, and came back to find ev­ery­one had for­got­ten him. He started writ­ing again and won the prize again in 2015, the first per­son, he said, to win it twice. {024-S06}
~ He would never take a gov­ern­ment award, and the Khan Market Liberal Award, he said, “will never be ac­cepted by me”. {024-J11}
stories.why: A prize can sus­tain a lonely con­trar­ian in­stead of re­ward­ing con­form­ity. Varma’s an­swer to elite awards is not to abol­ish prizes but to have many of them, com­pet­ing, so that lonely voices can be recog­nised. {024-C09}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his two Bastiat Prizes

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on judging a thinker by his library
stories.head: What did Adam Smith read?
body: Amit Varma’s writ­ing stu­dents some­times ask why Adam Smith, one of his great he­roes, writes prose that can be a bit turgid at times. {024-S03}

Varma’s an­swer is to look at what Smith had to work with. Gutenberg had brought the print­ing press and books, but it was still a small num­ber of elites who read. Anyone set­ting out to gain and make knowl­edge had a very small sam­ple to work with.
“Think of what he must have read. Think of the mod­els he would have had,” Varma said. Smith had no world of lit­er­a­ture on writ­ing, and no writ­ing cour­ses like Varma’s.
~ Yet the ideas Smith came up with are re­mark­able, and to Varma that makes his achieve­ment even greater.
stories.why: Judge thinkers by what they had to read. Smith built re­mark­able ideas from a tiny sam­ple; today any­one with hunger can learn any­thing, which is why Varma wishes he were fif­teen now. {#fifteen}

quiz.a: He was a clerk in a patent of­fice, with no re­search fund­ing.

quiz.q: According to Josh Felman, what is putting one child through an American college like?
quiz.a: Buying a brand new BMW every year and rolling it off a cliff.

quiz.q: Why did Grigori Perelman refuse to publish his proof in a journal?
quiz.a: A proof is right or wrong; a journal’s brand name changes noth­ing.

quiz.q: Which essay by Agnes Callard explains why academic writing is so turgid?
quiz.a: *Publish and Perish*, which blames the in­cen­tives of ten­ure and jour­nals.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 24. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Grigori Perelman (George Bergman, CC BY-SA 4.0); Christopher Hitchens (ensceptico, CC BY 2.0); George Orwell (Cassowary Colorizations, CC BY 2.0); Bryan Caplan (Simultaneous movement, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.creator: Paul Tucker
shelf.why: It cov­ers the softer, ad­vanced-economy ver­sion of the prob­lem: power wielded by un­elected of­fi­cials, with checks and bal­ances weak­en­ing.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Publish and Perish
shelf.creator: Agnes Callard
shelf.why: Callard uses an economist’s tool, in­cen­tives, to ex­plain turgid aca­demic writ­ing.

shelf.title: Politics and the English Language
shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: Orwell’s primer on clear writ­ing, which shows the link runs both ways: writ­ing clearly forces you to think clearly, and jar­gon is where mud­dled think­ing hides.

shelf.title: Social conformity despite individual preferences for distinctiveness
shelf.creator: Paul Smaldino and Joshua Epstein
shelf.why: The title cap­tures what hap­pens on cam­pus.

shelf.title: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Paul Graham’s two-axis map of thinkers (con­ven­tional or in­de­pen­dent, pas­sive or ag­gres­sive) that sin­gles out the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded as the loud­est voices and the real ob­sta­cle to new ideas.

shelf.title: Marginal Revolution
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: The blog Amit thinks has been the best in the world for 15 years: two econ­o­mists think­ing aloud in clear prose every day, a model for aca­demics and bet­ter sense-making than a newspaper’s eco­nom­ics pages.

shelf.title: How Cormac McCarthy Became a Copy-Editor for Scientific Books and One of the Most Influential Articles in Economics
shelf.why: The story of nov­el­ist Cormac McCarthy clean­ing up a sci­en­tific paper, which Ajay says ev­ery­one in academia should study as a les­son in how re­search should be writ­ten.

shelf.title: Do prestigious science journals attract bad science?
shelf.creator: Julia Belluz
shelf.why: Background for Ajay’s ar­gu­ment that top-journal pa­pers are often weaker be­cause re­searchers pour their en­ergy into gam­ing the sys­tem rather than into the knowl­edge.

shelf.title: Manifold Destiny
shelf.creator: Sylvia Nasar and David Gruber
shelf.why: Further read­ing on Perelman, the math­e­ma­ti­cian who re­fused both jour­nals and the mil­lion-dollar prize.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

shelf.title: If You Are a Creator, This Is Your Time
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s five rea­sons this is a good time for cre­ators: they own the means of pro­duc­tion, need no gate­keep­ers, face no con­straint of form, reach au­di­ences di­rectly and can mon­e­tise di­rectly.

shelf.title: The Incredible Insights of Timur Kuran (Episode 349, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The long ver­sion of Timur Kuran’s ideas, from pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion and the Soviet col­lapse to the long di­ver­gence.

shelf.title: How to Think About Cricket (and Life) (Episode 19, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s con­trar­ian ideas on cricket strat­egy and tac­tics, first de­vel­oped in 2008 and still not well un­der­stood, which he says hold truly novel in­sights.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: Three Great Leaps by Firms (Episode 22, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ first episode purely about firms: three com­pa­nies that sur­prised them by how they changed, and why firms, where mod­ern pro­duc­tion hap­pens, are where knowl­edge must flow.

shelf.title: Homeopathic Faith
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is an ex­am­ple of the crit­i­cal eye that Ajay says aca­demics must now turn on them­selves.

shelf.title: Are You Just One Version of Yourself (Episode 3, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On whether char­ac­ter is con­tin­gent and whether we can ever know our­selves: a small change in brain chem­istry, as with Phineas Gage, can make you a dif­fer­ent per­son.

laughs.text: The open­ing: Amit says Ajay keeps teas­ing him, ‘Amit, I’m a card-carrying econ­o­mist. I’ve done a PhD and all of that. You’ve stud­ied noth­ing, you’re a fool’, yet here he is agree­ing that de­grees mean noth­ing. Ajay con­cedes: ‘Across twenty short episodes, Amit has changed my views.’

Ajay quotes Edison: ‘ge­nius is 1% in­spi­ra­tion and 99% per­spi­ra­tion.’ Amit: ‘Edison didn’t have air con­di­tion­ing in his time.’ Ajay, sweat­ing through the shoot: ‘And his cam­eras did not over­heat in the Indian heat.’
Josh Felman’s line, re­layed by Ajay: putting one child through col­lege in America ‘in­volves buy­ing one brand new BMW car every year and rolling it off the edge of a cliff.’
Ajay on the cre­den­tial as a lux­ury good: ‘You get a Louis Vuitton bag, it is some IIT de­gree, and then you’re sup­posed to be done.’
Amit on aca­demic silos: ‘you’ll be writ­ing about wheat pro­duc­tion in Arizona be­tween the years 1863 to 1865.’
Amit, un­fil­tered: ‘I think aca­demics is ut­terly ir­rel­e­vant. It’s a cir­cle jerk. It’s pompous old farts talk­ing to other pompous old farts.’
Ajay on what the in­ter­net would have meant for a self-taught ge­nius: ‘Today, Ramanujan would have been dol­ing out his gems, one blog ar­ti­cle at a time.’
Amit, cling­ing to his two Bastiat Prizes against Ajay’s anti-prize stance: ‘But do not take my two can­dle­sticks away from me.’
Amit on in­dus­trial-era school­ing: ‘mon­keys can climb trees, but you’re also putting fish through an exam of how to climb trees. It’s not fair, it’s crazy.’

‘Publication orientation’: the dreaded phrase older aca­demics use to beat ide­al­ism out of young re­searchers. In Ajay’s words, ‘you’re sup­posed to or­ga­nize your life around shut up and get the pub.’
Ajay quotes ‘a beau­ti­ful quotation’: ‘the process of ed­u­ca­tion is not fill­ing a pail, the process of ed­u­ca­tion is kin­dling a fire.’

Ajay quotes lines from a song­writer both hosts think a lot about, to argue against win­ner-takes-all prizes: ‘and I won and I won big once. And I paid the cost. Inside I felt like I was car­ry­ing the bro­ken spir­its of all the other ones who lost.’
Sturgeon’s Law, in­voked by Amit against sniffi­ness about YouTube cre­ators: ‘Ninety five per­cent of ev­ery­thing is crap’, and it al­ways has been.
